|---|---|---|---|---|
| id | `darkpsy` | `twilight` | `fullon` | `progressive` |
| BPM (contract) | 148–160 | 145–150 | 140–148 | 130–140 |
| BPM (knowledge-layer note) | 140–155, Wikipedia 150+ | 145–150 | 140–148 | 130–140 |
| Template | 155 | 148 | 146 | 138 |
| Bars / minutes | 288 / 7.43 | 288 / 7.78 | 272 / 7.45 | 288 / 8.35 |
| Tracks (old templates) | 19 | 19 | 18 | 17 |
| Notes played | 9 972 | 10 083 | 6 623 | 5 437 |
| Density (notes/bar) | 34.62 | 35.01 | 24.35 | 18.88 |
| Sample entries (old templates) | 72 | 72 | 47 | 43 |
| Bass gate (`codigo`) | 35–50 ms | 45–60 ms | 50–65 ms | 55–75 ms |
| Grammars (`codigo`) | kbbb, kbb, kb-b | kbbb, kbb, kb-b | kbbb (turns with fifths and octaves), kbb | kbb, kbbb, offbeat |
| Structure (`codigo`) | Intro 32, Groove 64, Development 64, Break 32, Return 64, Outro 32 | same | Intro 32, Groove 32, Development 64, Break **48**, Return 64, Outro 32 | Intro 32, Groove 64, Development 64, Break 32, **Main** 64, Outro 32 |

A **BPM disagreement in darkpsy**: 148–160 in Core's contract, 140–155 in the knowledge-layer note. Open.

title: Style sheet — Darkpsy, Twilight, Full-on, Progressive psy · Each one's signature (`online`)
text:
- **Darkpsy** — tight KBBB in E, 16ths with rolls, acid and growl alternating; tension, organic and dark. Close to
  dark psycore: GLITCH, GROWL (Grit) and BODY strong; the engine compressor on the drums + bass group.
  The 2026-11-08 guide (`externo`): KBBB often in E or F, 16ths with 1/32 rolls; the bass gate a little longer than
  in dark psycore (35–50 ms) for a fuller roll at 150. In Core: W-Core *Dark Plonk* or *Dark Rubber* for the dark
  tone, or *Saw Roller* for a cleaner roll — shorten the notes to the gate; W-Core *Swamp Siren* or *Acid Needle* (a hi-tech preset) for
  the acid; Core FX *Dark spiral* or *Twilight swirl* (its frequency-shift delay) on the lead bus for echoes that drift out of tune; Core FX
  *Tension phaser* or *Hats flange* (its Modulate module) for slow dark movement in the background layers.
- **Twilight** — low KBBB in F♯, hats with holes, glitch percussion, a twisted lead that comes back in the break. Like
  full-on but darker: GROWL on the bass middle, Core FX *Twilight swirl* on the accents.
- **Full-on** — a kick with more body, bright KBBB in G with fifths, a G-minor melody that carries the break, plucks.
  Proposed chain: lead (W-Core *Squelch 303* or *Acid Needle*) → resonant filter (acid, resonance 50–75 %) → D-Core · Delay
  *Acid 3/16*; hats with Core FX *Hats flange*.
- **Progressive psy** — round bass in A (KBB, KBBB in the main part), shuffled hats, Am–G–F arpeggio, pads, hypnosis
  and long evolution. **Little chaos**: delays and BODY's width, no GLITCH or heavy drive.

Signature sources: `core-template.md:64-72` and
`COMBINAR-PLUGINS-E-SAMPLES.md:47-56`.

title: Style sheet — Darkpsy, Twilight, Full-on, Progressive psy · Common to the four
text:
- Arithmetic: 1/16 = `15000/BPM` ms → 94–115 ms between 160 and 130 BPM. The 25–50 ms gate still works; at ~145 BPM
  the kick→bass ducking works (which is why these templates duck the bass on the kick)
  (`core-template.md:74-80`).
- Kick and bass **from the same pack**, with the bass cut short.
- Master not approved yet; HP 30 Hz and mono below 120 Hz as a proposal (`online`).

title: Style sheet — Darkpsy, Twilight, Full-on, Progressive psy · What closes this sheet
text:
1. Diogo giving a BPM range and a character per sub-genre (the only thing missing for this to be a decision and not a survey).
2. One heard template per sub-genre, with approved levels.
3. Leads heard and approved on W-Core · Wave.

title: Style sheet — Psytrance
text:
# Style sheet — Psytrance

Main source: `inbox/core-improvements/conhecimento/estilos/psytrance.md`.
**No template of its own**: `dados/estilos.json` has `templates: []` for psytrance, and Core has one template per
sub-genre (Darkpsy, Twilight, Full-on, Progressive) — see `psy-subgenres.md`.

title: Style sheet — Psytrance · Identity
text:
138–160 BPM, typical 145 — `externo`, because Diogo includes psytrance in the focus but gave no range (`:13`). Rolling,
more melodic leads, and the base of the sample library (`:9`). The genre has many sub-styles; this sheet is the
common trunk, and the per-family profiles are in the online survey
(`dados/online.json`: 17 sub-styles, 29 findings, 15 sources).

title: Style sheet — Psytrance · Rhythm and bass
text:
- Grammars kbbb, kbb, kb-b. At 145 BPM a 1/16 is ~103 ms, so Core's 25–50 ms gate keeps the bass dry here too
  (`hipotese`, `:24`).
- A full-on kick is longer and fuller than a dark psycore one: "you don't make darkpsy with a full-on kick"
  (`externo`, `:29`). Kick an octave below the bass, its decay ending where the bass starts; fundamental 50–70 Hz (`:35`).
- No sub in the bass: HP 60–80 Hz, the kick owns everything below 80 Hz (`:36`).
- **Sidechain**: at ~145 BPM it is used on the bass — 4:1 to 8:1, attack 0.01–0.1 ms, release 80–120 ms, 6–10 dB of
  reduction per kick, hold 30–50 ms, recovery 60–80 ms. It stops working above ~200 BPM. The limit is the BPM, not the
  style (`online`, `:37`, `:41`). In Core: the track's **Ducking** (*Tight* 4 dB, *Pump* 8 dB, *Soft* 3 dB;
  values).

title: Style sheet — Psytrance · Bass recipe at 145 (`online`, `:31`)
text:
Osc A saw + osc B saw at +12, no sub; mono, no portamento; an amplitude envelope with no attack, full sustain,
decay ~140 ms (120–160) and release 20–40 ms; a 12 dB low-pass at 180–260 Hz with 10–15 % resonance; drive 15–25 %;
a filter envelope with ~40 ms decay and 15–25 % depth (above 40 % it becomes acid); a slow 4–8-bar LFO on the cutoff
at 5–8 %. In Core this is a **W-Core** bass preset (*Saw Roller*, *Saw Roller Low*, values): `tone` for the
low-pass, ENV 2 → tone for the envelope depth, `env2Decay` for its decay, the note gate for the length.

Note: the same source asks for a **velocity crescendo 95/108/120** on the three B notes, the opposite of Core's
templates (0.9 / 0.72 / 0.8 — `codigo`, `geral.md:17`). Until Diogo decides, the code wins. An FL Studio tutorial (2026-11-07) keeps all four 16ths and lets the velocity rise toward the end of each beat: see technique cards.

title: Style sheet — Psytrance · Structure and arrangement (`externo`)
text:
Phrases of 8 or 16 bars; a long breakdown with melody and FX in the middle of the track; the kick out for one bar
before the drop; change something every 32 bars, leads and rhythms every 8, layers every 4–8; tracks between 6 and
10 minutes (`:17-20`). Micro-timing (delay by 2–5 ms, or push ~30 ticks early) is written as a **variation to try,
not a rule** (`:25`).

title: Style sheet — Psytrance · Core plugins
text:
W-Core · Wave for the bass (bass presets) and the leads, or the Sampler with Diogo's samples for the bass.
W-Core's acid presets (*Squelch 303*, *Acid Needle*) or the engine filter for the acid/303; **PULSE** on pads and leads; Core FX's Modulate (*Hats flange*, *Twilight motion*) and
**D-Core · Delay** *Acid 3/16* are **strong** in twilight, progressive and full-on.
GROWL is strong in dark and avoided in progressive.

title: Style sheet — Psytrance · Samples
text:
A long kick (one beat = 414 ms at 145); KBBB bass and loops at 145/175; most of the library is full-on
(`hipotese`, `:165-175`). Query the sample database with `style = 'psytrance'`.

title: Style sheet — Psytrance · Status and what is missing
text:
All `externo` or `hipotese`. Master not approved yet; BPM and structure to be confirmed by Diogo; no levels and no
measured reference (`:41-42`, `:198-200`). The style with least knowledge **from this PC**: what exists came from
genre sources. It closes with: (1) Diogo giving a range and a character per sub-genre; (2) one heard template per
sub-genre; (3) approved levels and master.

title: Style sheet — Slambient
text:
# Style sheet — Slambient

Main source: `inbox/core-improvements/conhecimento/estilos/slambient.md`.
Core templates: `slambient` (300), `-minimal` (240),
`-dense` (360), `-extreme` (450).

title: Style sheet — Slambient · Identity
text:
180–500+ BPM, typical 300 (`decisao_diogo`). **It is fast music with a deep, soft kick** — the half-time feel comes from
the kick and the sub, not the tempo. Soft deep kick, dense sub, drones and textures, layers instead of drops, no lead,
cymbals almost inaudible (`decisao_diogo`).

There is no online definition of this style: the definition is Diogo's. The 90–120 BPM psychill is **not** Core's
slambient (`:217-218`). It is also the style with no measured reference at all — S-G2.

title: Style sheet — Slambient · Rhythm
text:
- Kick on the four beats, gate 140 ticks (100 in `-extreme`) (`codigo`, `:36`).
- Bass: kbb / kbbb / offbeat, a note of 0.55–0.7 of the gap, at most 25–45 ms, root MIDI 23–30 (B0–F♯1) (`codigo`, `:35`).
- Hats: a soft offbeat pulse, steps 2/6/10/14, **no rolls** (`codigo`, `:37-38`); tone 5.5–7 kHz, closed
  decay 16–24, open 250–350 (`:46-47`).
- Distant percussion on steps 5/13/27, with reverb 0.95 mix 0.55 (`codigo`, `:39`).
- A low boom every 4 bars: 90→30 Hz with 900 ms decay and reverb 1.0 (`codigo`, `:40`).

title: Style sheet — Slambient · Sound
text:
- Engine kick: pitchStart 110–150, pitchEnd 34–40, pitchDecay 18–32, ampDecay 65–115, click 0.02–0.08,
  drive 0.05–0.12 (`codigo`, `:44`); EQ HP 25, +2 @55, LP 3.5 kHz so it does not click (`:54`).
- Engine bass: envAmount 2–3, filterDecay 35–45, decay 36–44, release 6–9, drive 0.25–0.35, **sub 0.7–0.85 with
  octave −1** (`codigo`, `:45`). The accepted exception to the "rolling bass without sub" rule. In Core:
  a sample of Diogo's in the Sampler or the **W-Core** bass preset *Deep Pulse* (values), with the mood
  *Cathedral*.
- Bass chain: saturation 6/0.4/−2 → EQ −3 dB @400 Q0.8 → utility width 0.6 with mono below 160 Hz (`codigo`, `:55`).
- Texture: a granular bed at +1 octave, drive 0.7, delay 0.1875 feedback 0.7 ping-pong, reverb 1.0 mix 0.6 preDelay 50
  (`codigo`, `:49`). Drone an octave above the root, LP 1200, reverb 1.0 mix 0.7 preDelay 60 (`:50`).
  In Core: W-Core · Wave drones (*Abyss Drone*, *Ghost Wind*, *Glass Cloud*, *Frozen Dust*) and its grain.
- Automation: cutoff multiplier 1.5; master sweep up to 400 Hz (`codigo`, `:61`).
- Core plugins: **Core FX** for long tails (*Haunted*, *Huge space*, *Ghost shimmer*; shimmer with care) and
  **R-Core · Reverb** as a shared bus; **BODY** for width; **PUNCH** only **to soften, never to click**; **Core FX**
  *Haunted ensemble* (chorus) for a wider, thicker sound. Avoid: GROWL, METAL's crush, ZAP, PUNCH's Clip, and any saturation on the
  master (`:84-177`). **Gap:** no reverse-swell or convolution effect in Core (F-Core phase 2).
- Style racks: `haunted`, `ghost-voice`, `abyss-boom`, `slow-unease` now played natively (list).

title: Style sheet — Slambient · Structure
text:
320 bars: Intro 32 (1), Layers 64 (2), Transform 64 (3), Reduction 32 (1), Deep 96 (3), Outro 32 (1) (`codigo`, `:26`).
Layers instead of drops; an 8-bar riser (2→24); drone up to energy 3; granular texture from energy 2
(`codigo`, `:27-31`). Break ×0.67–0.75 and drop ×1.25–1.5 (300→450, 450→300, 240↔360) — the tempo changes are the
style's language (`codigo`, `:14`).

title: Style sheet — Slambient · Levels and master
text:
**Nothing approved.** Proposed levels (`estudo`, `:65`): kick −0.45, bass −5.5, hats −16.1, texture −22.1, riser −18.0 —
and the file explicitly warns not to take them as approved (`:204`).

Proposed master (`estudo`, `:71`): HP 20 (the absolute minimum — the sub lives in 18–46 Hz), shelf EQ −1 @40, notch @210 Q1.2,
LP 14k, compressor 1.6:1 att 30, utility width 1.3 with mono < 100, limiter −1.4, **no saturation for streaming**;
a club variant with saturation 3/0.2 and limiter −0.8. The Core-only template's master is on its
template page.

title: Style sheet — Slambient · Samples
text:
A kick with no click, 34–40 Hz, sub; at 300 BPM a beat is 200 ms and at 450 it is 133 ms, so the tail must be short
even though it is deep. A bass with a high `subRatio`, B0–F♯1, an octave down, 25–45 ms. Dark hats 5.5–7 kHz — or none.
FX `long, dark, sub` (`hipotese`, `:189-199`). The library has almost only pads, FX and impacts for this style
(see the sample database).

title: Style sheet — Slambient · Out of the style (`estudo`, `:209`)
text:
A clicky hi-tech kick; a dense KBBB with high drive; aggressive straight 16ths; a lead or acid in call and response;
saturation on the streaming master; a master HP above 20 Hz (it cuts the sub).

title: Style sheet — Slambient · Status and what is missing
text:
BPM, character and structure: `decisao_diogo` / `codigo`. Levels, master, samples and plugin fit: `estudo` or
`hipotese`. Missing: an authorised reference from Diogo himself (S-G2), heard levels (S-G3), and confirming that the
450 BPM of `-extreme` still sounds like slambient.

title: Teaching priority — making KBBB and elastic bass with intent
text:
# Teaching priority — making KBBB and elastic bass with intent

Originally 2026-11-04 (AICORE `docs/knowledge/KBBB-E-ELASTIC-BASS.md`, core-main `affa84ab`); translated and updated
for Core-only. **Diogo's stated priority:** the AI must know how to build KBBB/elastic bass and make interesting
variations. EQ, effects and style classification support that goal. Everything below is curriculum and synthetic
examples; nothing has been trained or listened to.

title: Teaching priority — making KBBB and elastic bass with intent · 1. What the AI must learn
text:
KBBB is timing: a kick at the start of each beat and three bass notes on the following sixteenths. By itself it does
not define timbre. "Elastic bass" describes perceived articulation and movement, not one parameter nor a universal
grammar. It can come from a mix of filter/amplitude envelope, contrast of lengths and accents, timbre/harmonics, how
notes connect, and the interaction with the kick.

Read "more elastic" as a hypothesis to show in a few alternatives: filter movement, rhythmic articulation, and the
**Dive** pitch drop at note start. Do not always turn it into more release, more distortion or sidechain. Keep which
alternative Diogo approved and why; his personal meaning of "elastic" is learnt from evidence.

**In Core today:** B-Core · Bass is gone (core-main #240, 2026-11-08). The bass is a sample of Diogo's in the
**Sampler**, or **W-Core · Wave** (`wave`) with its bass presets (*Saw Roller*, *Full Speed Saw/Punch/Deep*,
*Dark Plonk/Rubber/Bite*, *Deep Pulse*); every knob and preset with its values is in
presets › W-Core. The simpler engine `bass` instrument has
`octave, sub, cutoff, resonance, envAmount, filterDecay, attack, decay, sustain, release, drive, level` and no glide.
Never invent `elastic`, `bounce` or `glide` arguments in a call: use the function registry's real arguments.

title: Teaching priority — making KBBB and elastic bass with intent · 2. Grammar and grid
text:
4/4, a 16-step grid, four steps per beat. K is the kick on its own track; b is bass; a dot is no bass. The kick is not
part of the bass track's notes.

| Family | One beat | One bar | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| KBBB | Kbbb | Kbbb Kbbb Kbbb Kbbb | The reference rolling engine |
| KBB | Kbb. | Kbb. Kbb. Kbb. Kbb. | More room at the end of the beat |
| KB-B | Kb.b | Kb.b Kb.b Kb.b Kb.b | A hole in the middle, a different feel |
| Offbeat | K.b. | K.b. K.b. K.b. K.b. | A sparser off-beat |
| Triplet | K + b at 1/3 and 2/3 of the beat | Does not fit the binary 16-step grid | A ternary variant, not KBBB |

These five grammars exist in the randomizer and in P-Core; each style allows a subset. The randomizer picks menus and
turns; it proves neither creativity nor taste. P-Core writes the shape directly.

With PPQ 960: quarter = 960 ticks, sixteenth = 240, bar = 3840; KBBB has bass at ticks 240/480/720, repeated every 960.
An eighth-note triplet uses 320 and 640 within the beat. Read the real PPQ and bar before composing.

title: Teaching priority — making KBBB and elastic bass with intent · 3. Eight axes of musical variation
text:
| Axis | Interesting variation | Property to keep | How |
|---|---|---|---|
| Accents | Three different velocities, shifting weight between notes | Same timing/pitches when only articulation is asked | Velocity per note; check the instrument's real response |
| Gate | Short–medium–short or the reverse | No unintended collisions, no BPM change | Note length per event, observed release |
| Silence | Drop one note at the phrase end, then return | KBBB stays recognisable, kick fixed | Omit one specific note; do not turn everything into KBB |
| Pitch | A short turn, fifth/octave or approved approach | Tonic/scale/intent and the sub's register | Pitch per note; control jumps, do not move every note |
| Microtiming | Delay one note slightly for bounce | The kick's pulse and room for the next note | Tick moved within explicit limits; no general random jitter |
| Envelope/timbre | More filter movement without more drive | Body, level and approved rhythm | Real W-Core knobs (ENV 2 → tone, `env1Decay`, `tone`…) and automation only when needed |
| Question/answer | A repeated, then a small answer B | Main identity and phrase length | 2/4-bar patterns or alternating clips |
| Macro form | Evolve over 8/16 bars and come back | Section/targets/tempo of the request | Patterns/clips/automation in the isolated scope |

Vary one or two axes per proposal, with an identifiable intent. "Interesting" does not mean more notes, octaves,
distortion or random numbers. The AI must explain briefly the audible difference expected and what it kept.

title: Teaching priority — making KBBB and elastic bass with intent · 4. Starting exercise library
text:
The synthetic pattern bank has 12 explicit constructions for demonstration and
structural checks. They are not sound presets, approved examples nor a final dataset. Root MIDI 33 and 146 BPM are
fixture context only. The same 12 shapes are P-Core's bass patterns (patterns).

| ID | Goal | Main change |
|---|---|---|
| kbbb-anchor | Make the reference | Three equal bass notes per beat |
| kbbb-accent-wave | Bounce while keeping the notes | Velocity 0.72/0.52/0.64 per beat |
| kbbb-gate-wave | Vary elasticity by articulation | Gate 90/150/110 ticks |
| kbbb-breath | Open room before the return | Omit only the bar's last note |
| kbbb-fifth-turn | A small harmonic turn | A fifth on the last note only; needs harmonic acceptance |
| kbbb-octave-answer | A register answer | Octave on the last bass note; compare the sub's body |
| kbbb-microbounce | Subtle time bounce | Second note of each trio 8 ticks late |
| kbb-spaced | Compare a more open grammar | Two notes per beat, room at the end |
| kb-b-syncopated | Compare silence in the middle | First and third notes of the trio |
| triplet-contrast | Teach binary vs ternary | Bass at 1/3 and 2/3 of the beat |
| kbbb-two-bar-answer | Make question/answer | First bar anchor, second with a small answer |
| kbbb-eight-bar-evolution | Evolve without losing identity | 1–3 anchor, 4 breathes, 5–7 accents, 8 answers |

After checking these alone, build combinations: gate+accent, microtiming+silence, answer+filter. Compare each with the
anchor and with the last approved version, not just with another extreme variation.

title: Teaching priority — making KBBB and elastic bass with intent · 5. Elasticity recipes — hypotheses to test
text:
- **E1 — elastic through the filter:** keep notes/gates and drive; try a filter envelope with more contrast, change
  decay gradually and compensate level. More envelope amount can mean more aggression, not more quality.
- **E2 — elastic through articulation:** fixed timbre, alternate gates/accents inside the trio. Compare
  short–medium–short with medium–short–medium. Choose by the feeling of return and room, not maximum length.
- **E3 — elastic through bounce:** keep BPM/kick and move one position a few ticks, with margin before the next onset.
  Microtiming is not randomness; keep the stable relation that works.
- **E4 — melodic elastic:** a small pitch/register answer over the tonic, with clear returns; on W-Core a short
  envelope link to `pitch` gives a pitch drop at note start (plonk). Overlap/legato can change retriggering and needs checking.
- **E5 — elastic through dynamics/ducking:** if pumping is asked, try envelope/sidechain with a recovery that fits the
  real gap (the Ducking presets, presets). Ducking is not a mandatory replacement for
  a filter envelope.

Compare E1/E2 first with a fixed kick. For "the movement is good, but it got dirty": keep the movement and reduce the
distortion source, check resonance and level, without changing the grammar. For "more bounce, not brighter": try
articulation/timing and do not open the cutoff by reflex.

title: Teaching priority — making KBBB and elastic bass with intent · 6. Time, tail and limits
text:
Gate conversion: `lengthTicks = round(gateMs × BPM × PPQ / 60000)`. Use the section's local tempo, including tempo
maps. A MIDI note's length is not the audio's total length: release, plugin, sample and effects can carry on.

At 146 BPM and PPQ 960, 120 ticks ≈ 51.37 ms; at 240 BPM, 31.25 ms. Reusing ticks without deciding whether to keep
physical length or groove proportion changes the articulation. Recheck when the BPM changes.

For KBBB the last bass note must leave the intended room before the next kick. Compute the next event's onset/gate and
judge the real tail. The style cards' nominal gate is the algorithm's dry reference, not a universal limit for elastic
bass. For intended legato use another recipe; do not "fix" an authorised overlap as if it were always a defect.

Do not raise the tempo for energy. Do not use HP/sidechain to hide a colliding pattern. Do not deduce the sound's tail
from the note or `release` alone when the source is an unknown sample.

title: Teaching priority — making KBBB and elastic bass with intent · 7. Doing it in Core
text:
1. Read track, pattern, clips, selection, local tempo and relevant knobs; find every use of the pattern. Note the
   invariants: kick, BPM, key, timbre or movement already approved.
2. If the change is for one region only, isolate it first: editing a shared pattern changes every clip using it.
3. Build the variation as explicit notes (P-Core shape, or the pattern editor), checking ticks/length/pitch/velocity
   and the phrase limit.
4. Use P-Core for composition, W-Core's knobs and presets (or the Sampler) for the sound, automation for change over time. Changing the
   whole sound is not needed to vary gates.
5. *Edit > Randomize* is for exploring within the style (seed/axes/strength); it does not guarantee a specific
   variation nor protect an arbitrary region.
6. As an AI proposal: the calls go to `inbox/`, Core checks them, and Diogo presses Apply (one Undo step). Never write
   the project directly (the bridge).
7. Re-read and compare against the invariants; render or listen at matched gain when audio is available; otherwise
   say "implemented and structurally checked", never "approved".

title: Teaching priority — making KBBB and elastic bass with intent · 8. Data to collect
text:
For each episode: the request in plain words, source pattern/sound/tempo, constraints, proposed variation, real calls,
result, feedback per dimension and correction. Tell apart "like the rhythm", "don't like the timbre", "good
elasticity", "too bright", "lost body" and "good alone, bad with kick".

Priority targets: make the anchor; produce 2–3 contrasting alternatives when asked; continue a phrase; transform only
one region; keep an approved dimension; repair an overlap; recognise when there is no sound evidence. Error/recovery
examples matter; never train rejected answers as ideals. Do not keep hidden reasoning: the stated intent, structured
change, invariants, results and feedback are enough.

title: Teaching priority — making KBBB and elastic bass with intent · 9. Judging creative skill and execution
text:
- **Structural:** notes inside the pattern, correct PPQ, no unintended collision, invariants kept, correct edit
  limits, no effect outside the region, valid calls. The bank checks structure only; it is not a sound benchmark.
- **Musical:** KBBB identity recognisable when asked, audible intent, bounce/elasticity, kick/bass consistency,
  contrast between alternatives, phrase arc and return. Blind human comparison at matched level; ask for separate
  feedback on timbre and rhythm. A structurally correct version can be musically worse.
- **Learning:** on new requests, apply a fitting transformation without always copying the same turn or tonic. Do not
  define success by random diversity or lower loss.

Until there are approved sound examples, the elasticity recipes stay hypotheses.

title: Core's music styles — reference for teaching the AI
text:
# Core's music styles — reference for teaching the AI

Originally written 2026-11-04 (AICORE `docs/knowledge/ESTILOS-MUSICAIS-E-PRODUCAO.md`, core-main `affa84ab`); kept and
translated here, Core-only. A static reading of code and JSON: no playback, listening, spectral measurement or plugin
test. This is domain knowledge for AICORE, not confirmed personal preferences nor an approved dataset.

**Three levels of evidence:** OBS = value observed in the app; REC = editorial production advice, to try and validate;
PEND = needs references or expert listening. REC advice describes useful, plausible practice, not a statistic about
"what all producers use". No EQ curve is right just because it belongs to a genre.

**Teaching priority set by Diogo:** KBBB and elastic bass. Start with building and varying
those basses creatively and correctly; use the EQ/effects profiles below as context.

title: Core's music styles — reference for teaching the AI · 1. What the app actually uses
text:
| Family in Core | Randomizer BPM OBS | Templates and BPM OBS | Style card's nominal gate OBS |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dark psycore | 200–260 | 210 spaced, 225 base, 240 dense, 255 syncopated | 32–45 ms |
| Hi-tech | 170–220 | 175 clean, 190 base, 205 dense, 220 triplets | 40–50 ms |
| Slambient | 180–500 | 240 deep, 300 base, 360 dense, 450 extreme | 25–45 ms |
| Darkpsy | 148–160 | 155 | 35–50 ms |
| Twilight | 145–150 | 148 | 45–60 ms |
| Full-on | 140–148 | 146 | 50–65 ms |
| Progressive psy | 130–140 | 138 | 55–75 ms |

These are the implementation's ranges, not universal genre borders nor global sequencer limits. "Dark" is ambiguous:
tell Darkpsy from Dark psycore before changing tempo or groove. "Progressive" here means Progressive psy, not
progressive house or rock. "Psytrance" can mean the whole family, not an eighth style card. Slambient has its own
definition in this project; do not equate it with slow ambient or a universal taxonomy.

The gate above is the randomizer's choice, not a guaranteed physical length of the sample's or plugin's tail. The
loaded document is the operational truth.

title: Core's music styles — reference for teaching the AI · 2. What the templates actually set
text:
Every Core-only template's tracks, effects with their values and master chain are in the generated
template pages, read from the files Core loads. Units: EQ frequencies in Hz, EQ gains
in dB. OBS (`engine/src/dsp/effects.cpp`): the engine Delay's `time` is in beats; `delay.time=0.75` is 0.75 of a
quarter note, not 750 ms. Convert at the local BPM; other plugins may use other units (ECHO and D-Core use note
divisions — see presets).

Do not turn these defaults into "the best mix". Low boosts, master cuts, limiters and compression depend on the source
levels. One template compressor may be tone/glue and another may have a sidechain detector: the same name does not
prove the same job.

title: Core's music styles — reference for teaching the AI · 3. EQ vocabulary and common diagnosis — REC
text:
| Approximate zone | Frequent role | Intervention to test | Sign the intervention is wrong |
|---|---|---|---|
| Below 20–30 Hz | Infra/rumble, or intended energy | Gentle HP only if useless energy or headroom justifies it | Lost weight or kick phase; do not cut everything by reflex |
| 30–60 Hz | Sub/fundamental of kick/bass | Decide who owns the region; tuning, envelope and balance before boosting | Lots of level without definition; poor translation on small systems |
| 60–120 Hz | Body of bass/kick | Small wide adjustment or dynamic control when they overlap | Thin low end or artificial pumping |
| 120–250 Hz | Warmth/body and tail overlap | Shorten length/level or contextual EQ | Musical body lost by systematic cutting |
| 250–500 Hz | Body, possible build-up/boxiness | Wide 1–3 dB cut first, if it is really muddy | Hollow bass; texture with no substance |
| 500 Hz–1.5 kHz | Identity/notes, reading on small speakers | Review arrangement, harmonics and saturation before cutting | Sound disappears in mono or at low volume |
| 1.5–4 kHz | Attack, presence, intelligibility | Solve lead/percussion competition; dynamic cut if available | Lost articulation, or aggression and fatigue |
| 4–8 kHz | Click, aggressive brightness, sibilance | Tame peaks with level/EQ, or pick another sample | Lifeless hats; the kick's click no longer cuts through |
| 8–16 kHz | Air and texture of hats/reverbs | Subtle shelf when needed; control noise/aliasing at the source | Fragile, harsh or just louder mix |

Zones overlap; they are not fixed note tables. For a resonance, confirm the real frequency and use a fitting Q, without
stacking narrow notches out of habit. REC starting gains: wide ±1–3 dB changes; bigger corrections only with a
diagnosis. The neutral/bypass value is always a valid candidate. Remember the engine EQ's `midFreq` starts at 200 Hz
(a known gap).

title: Core's music styles — reference for teaching the AI · Chains per job — REC, with Core plugins
text:
- **Kick:** pick/tune the sound → envelope/tail → corrective EQ if needed → optional controlled saturation or clip
  (PUNCH for click and cut). Do not align every phase by a fixed number; check kick/bass interaction and polarity in
  context.
- **Rolling bass:** oscillator or sample and envelope (a W-Core bass preset or a sample in the Sampler) → tone/filter → moderate saturation (BODY,
  `saturation`) → EQ if needed → dynamic control / mono low end (`utility` monoBelow). Filtering before or after
  saturation gives different results; compare at matched gain.
- **Hats/percussion:** envelope and velocity editing first; HP only for unneeded energy, maybe harshness control;
  reverb/delay in doses that keep the groove (SPACE, ECHO).
- **Leads:** filter/EQ to make room for the low end → distortion/modulation by source (GROWL, Core FX's Modulate module and frequency-shift delay) → filtered
  delay/reverb (D-Core, R-Core). Lead synths are a **gap** until W-Core · Wave.
- **Pads/drones:** remove clashing lows, slow automation and ambience; width in the high layers, check mono. Do not
  remove the fundamental of a deliberately low drone.
- **Master:** compare headroom and reference at matched loudness; do not fix a kick/bass clash with a global cut or
  boost. Do not teach an "obligatory" LUFS nor apply a limiter per style without measuring.

title: Core's music styles — reference for teaching the AI · Darkpsy — 148–160 BPM in the app
text:
Frequent goal: tension, hypnosis, an organic/dark feel and continuous rolling. KBBB dominant, with KBB and deliberate
gaps. Explore alternating acid, growls and atmospheric layers, without putting every element in the centre at once.

EQ: keep definition between the kick's fundamental and the bass; look into 150–400 Hz build-up when several textures
enter. Keep 1–4 kHz for each moment's main voice; lively hats without constant excess at 6–10 kHz. Do not confuse
"dark" with a low-pass on the whole song.

Effects: controlled resonant filters, layered saturation, short/dotted delays and reverb on the atmospheres; automate
feedback and brightness per phrase. Bass/kick central and ambiences to the sides, mono checked. Sidechain can help an
overlap but does not replace a fitting envelope or sample.

Variations: more forest/organic (a language reference, not an existing Forest template), more acid, more percussive,
drier, more spacious. Change one axis at a time and keep what was approved. A more open break and a return with a
contrast of density, not just more volume.

title: Core's music styles — reference for teaching the AI · Twilight — 145–150 BPM in the app
text:
Goal: a night groove with twisted timbres, linking weight/dark with a melodic reading. KBBB with gappy hats, small
rhythmic answers and glitches; do not turn the whole phrase into a fill.

EQ: kick/bass body without filling 200–500 Hz; mid leads may ask for alternating room at 700 Hz–3 kHz. Treat glitch
harshness at 3–8 kHz one by one, without removing overall brightness. The groove depends as much on velocity and
silence as on the EQ curve.

Effects: short/ping-pong delay on chosen percussion, filters/modulation on the lead, growl with controlled saturation.
Alternate dry/wet between question and answer. A filtered delay in transitions adds depth without constantly crowding
the front.

Variations: more funky/percussive, darker, more melodic, more fragmented. Keep the bass's role and the structure;
micro-vary one answer every 4/8/16 bars, do not randomise everything.

title: Core's music styles — reference for teaching the AI · Full-on — 140–148 BPM in the app
text:
Goal: clear rolling, frontal energy and a memorable lead. The app has KBBB with fifths/octaves on the turns and a
melodic break. Do not assume Full-on always means euphoric or maximum highs.

EQ: kick body and bass reading live together through tuning/envelope/level; only clean real build-up at 200–400 Hz.
Leads with presence at 1–4 kHz, hats/air without fatigue. If the melody competes with the bass, treat register/voicing
before an aggressive high-pass.

Effects: synced delay and a moderate plate/hall on the lead, contrast of ambience in the break, occasional risers and
impacts; keep the attack on the return. Saturation for harmonics, not to replace headroom. Avoid delay on the sub
unless asked.

Variations: morning/melodic, a tenser night, more groove or more direct. Descriptive references to review with
examples; do not declare new categories implemented. Raise energy with arrangement and articulation, not only the
limiter.

title: Core's music styles — reference for teaching the AI · Progressive psy — 130–140 BPM in the app
text:
Goal: hypnosis, space and long evolution; a round bass, KBB/offbeat, and KBBB at peaks depending on the variant. Arp
and pads can develop slowly.

EQ: keep body at 50–150 Hz without overlap; clean pads/reverb hiding the groove at 150–500 Hz. Control the arp's mids
without emptying the harmony. A more discreet brightness can be a choice, not a defect to fix with a shelf.

Effects: a slow filter, delays on sends or automated mix, reverb with space and a useful pre-delay, moderate ducking
when needed. Compression with attack/release matched to the real envelope; "pumping" is an explicit aesthetic option.

Variations: minimal/hypnotic, more tribal/percussive, more melodic, more rolling. Build 16/32-bar arcs and bring layers
in gradually; do not demand a new element every bar. Do not swap it for progressive house because of the word.

title: Core's music styles — reference for teaching the AI · Dark psycore — 200–260 BPM in the app
text:
Goal: high intensity, short transients and articulation in very little time. KBBB/KBB/KB-B and chromatic turns; less
room between events makes tails and ambiences more critical.

EQ: a defined sub rather than simply a bigger one; check time overlap before cutting 200–500 Hz. Distortion can make
useful mids and also harshness at 2–8 kHz: compare against a matched bypass. Avoid stacking low boosts and saturation
on every element.

Effects: dry envelopes in the centre, filtered delays in the gaps/answers, layered atmospheres. Fast ducking or a
volume envelope can work if there is enough control; do not teach the false rule that sidechain stops working above
200 BPM. Release and detection must match the available gap.

Variations OBS: spaced 210, base 225, dense 240, syncopated 255. Faster does not automatically mean denser. Variation
REC: remove a bass note or hat, move an answer, change a turn; compare without changing kick, timbre and tempo at once.

title: Core's music styles — reference for teaching the AI · Hi-tech — 170–220 BPM in the app
text:
Goal: contrast, fast articulation, zaps/FM and audible changes with a readable bass. KBBB dominant, passages in
triplets and octaves; short pauses matter as much as rolls.

EQ: control the kick's click and the competition between leads and hats at 2–8 kHz; keep the harmonics that let the
bass read on small systems. Resonant zaps may need automation or local control instead of cutting the highs of the
whole mix.

Effects: short rhythmic delays, filtered ping-pong, small tails on the front lead and long ambiences only in chosen
parts. Feedback and resonance with limits; extreme effects need a clear return.

Variations OBS: clean 175, base 190, dense 205, triplets 220. REC: occasional stutter/ratchet (GLITCH), call and
answer, an octave jump, straight/triplet alternation. Do not raise rate/feedback/drive without compensating level and
testing intelligibility.

title: Core's music styles — reference for teaching the AI · Slambient — Core's own definition, 180–500 BPM
text:
In the app: fast music with a soft/deep kick, a dense bass, drones, textures and spatial transformation; no front lead
required. A high BPM does not mean a dance feel on every quarter: listen to the pulse, groupings and half-time feel.

EQ: manage infra/sub and overlapping tails; drones with intended low energy need a decision about role and dynamics,
not an automatic HP. Mid/high layers can be filtered for depth. Keep the body with room between layers instead of
widening everything.

Effects: more present reverbs/delays on textures, filtered returns, slow modulation and moderate saturation; keep the
low end readable. Extreme density may require fewer events and shorter tails, even if the genre asks for atmosphere.

Variations OBS: deep 240, base 300, dense 360, extreme 450. Substyle terms and outside consensus stay PEND. Ask Diogo
for a reference if the intent does not match this definition.

title: Core's music styles — reference for teaching the AI · 5. Tempo, gates and synced effects
text:
A quarter note lasts `60000/BPM` ms; a sixteenth `15000/BPM` ms; an eighth-note triplet `20000/BPM` ms. A dotted
eighth is 0.75 of a quarter. Confirm whether an effect uses beats, seconds, ms or a list of divisions before setting
any value.

| Reference BPM | Quarter ms | Sixteenth ms | Dotted eighth ms |
|---|---|---|---|
| 138 | 434.78 | 108.70 | 326.09 |
| 146 | 410.96 | 102.74 | 308.22 |
| 148 | 405.41 | 101.35 | 304.05 |
| 155 | 387.10 | 96.77 | 290.32 |
| 190 | 315.79 | 78.95 | 236.84 |
| 225 | 266.67 | 66.67 | 200.00 |
| 300 | 200.00 | 50.00 | 150.00 |
| 450 | 133.33 | 33.33 | 100.00 |

In a KBBB the bass notes fill the three sixteenths after the kick. A MIDI gate does not necessarily include release,
the sample's tail or reverb. Compare the real length up to the next relevant event; "it fits in the beat" is no proof.
When the BPM changes, check automation, delays and gate compensation, without changing approved tempos out of habit.

Tuning formula: `f = 440 × 2^((midi−69)/12)` Hz. An octave down doubles the period; compressing a sub very fast can
modulate/distort the waveform. Do not impose a fixed kick fundamental on every key. The perceived pitch of a swept
kick and kick/bass phase need observation and listening.

title: Core's music styles — reference for teaching the AI · 6. Variation and structure the AI must understand
text:
- Axes: bass rhythm, gate, hat grid/velocity, ghost kick, active roles, fills, tempo and timbre. The randomizer is not
  permission to change every axis for a simple correction.
- Phrases of 4/8/16/32 bars are useful units, not laws. Make contrast by removing/bringing back elements, register,
  filter, ambience and pauses.
- Intro/outro should be able to serve a DJ transition when that is the goal; a break/drop is not required for every
  intent. Use the existing sections before imposing another structure.
- Delay/reverb in transitions can run into the drop: check tails. Automation that returns to the wrong value is a
  defect, even when the effect alone sounds good.
- Harmonic variation does not mean changing key at random: identify tonic/scale/ambiguity and the role of dissonance.
  Reject key inference from a folder name alone when there is a conflict.

title: Core's music styles — reference for teaching the AI · 7. What to teach and how to make useful data (1)
text:
Keep three sources apart: this general retrievable knowledge; app facts/capabilities per version; Diogo's confirmed
preferences. A template does not prove personal taste. A new request that goes against the profile beats old habit.

| Skill | Synthetic task example | Behaviour to supervise | Failure to exclude |
|---|---|---|---|
| Disambiguation | "I want dark" | Tell Darkpsy from psycore by context or a short question | Jumping straight to 225 BPM |
| Contextual EQ | "The bass is muddy" | Check source, envelope/overlap, then propose a small checkable fix | Always cutting 300 Hz without looking |
| Preservation | "The movement is good, it got too dirty" | Keep the movement, reduce the distortion source and check level | Changing groove/BPM together with drive |
| Groove | "More rolling, without speeding up" | Change articulation/pattern within the approved tempo | Raising BPM to seem more energetic |
| Effects | "More space, kick stays dry" | Atmosphere on lead/texture, keep the kick | Indiscriminate global reverb |
| Limits | "EQ it like the reference" with no audio | Explain what can be observed, ask for a useful resource or propose a named hypothesis | Claiming to have heard/analysed without evidence |
| Contrary preference | "Today I want heavy distortion" | Respect the request and manage level, even if past taste was cleaner | Applying an old preference as an absolute rule |
| Integration | Effect/function not available | Read the function registry, offer an explicit alternative | Inventing parameters, plugins or buses |

For each goal, collect request/context, state before, functions, attempt/result, partial feedback, correction and state
after. Supervise only the reviewed next target; hidden reasoning is not needed. Group derived examples by episode so
splits stay clean.

Starting curriculum: recognise seven styles and variants → interpret goals and constraints → master tempo/gate/low end
→ EQ by diagnosis → effects/arrangement → correction from feedback → function use and checking. Prioritise frequent
errors and diversity, not thousands of paraphrases of the same seven cards.

title: Core's music styles — reference for teaching the AI · 7. What to teach and how to make useful data (2)
text:
Memory keeps specific tastes and evidence; retrieval provides these cards when relevant. The LoRA learns technical
behaviour, language and contextual application; avoid memorising a fixed curve per style. Do not resend this whole
document on every request: retrieve the style section + role/problem + the functions actually needed.

title: Core's music styles — reference for teaching the AI · 8. Coverage, sources and research still missing
text:
Sources read in the fixed snapshot: `templates/*.core-template.json`; `app/domain/src/randomize.cpp` (seven style
cards, grammars, gates and tempo limits); `app/domain/src/samples.cpp` (styles/tags metadata and suggestions);
`tools/templates/make_templates.py` (recipes; not run — the shipped JSON wins).

REC advice is an editorial technical synthesis, not a finished bibliographic or statistical survey. To call a setting
"the most common" needs a representative corpus with sources.

Next musical check: pick authorised references per style, note intent and role of the elements, compare at matched
loudness, test in mono and on several systems, review with an experienced producer. Log era/branch/key/BPM and sample,
without copying unauthorised audio or datasets.

Next taxonomy extension: Forest, Goa, Suomisaundi, psybient/psydub and others only after a request, references and a
specific survey. They are not counted as implemented styles.

title: Technique cards
text:
# Technique cards

Production techniques gathered from tutorials and research (AICORE `docs/knowledge/*.md` and `_local-wip`,
2026-11-04/05), translated and rewritten for **Core's own plugins**. Every card is a **candidate** (`hipotese`): not
yet tried in Core, not approved by ear. The tutorials used other DAWs and third-party plugins; each card says which
Core plugin plays the same musical role, or marks a **gap**.

How to use a card: pick the one that matches the intent, change one thing at a time, compare at similar level,
keep the original, and log what was heard. The AI proposes a card as Core function calls; nothing changes before
Apply (how plugins work).

Contents: Paths per style · Dark hi-tech workflow ·
Hi-tech space and impact ·
Hi-tech arrangement and bounce ·
Beep and pluck · Kick and stereo low end ·
Percussion · FX, risers, voice, impacts ·
Long synth one-shots · Lead pluck to intro texture ·
Psycore, psytrance, slambient recipes ·
Psytrance at 145 from FL Studio ·
Psytrance acid lead at 140 · Master and synth review

title: Technique cards · Paths per style (1)
text:
**Hi-tech — contrast, precision, movement.**
1. Base: listen to kick and bass at the real BPM; fix the bass articulation, then add hats, shaker and fills. For
   tension try a short pause or a hat run, one change at a time (dark hi-tech,
   KBBB).
2. Timbre: a beep and a pluck from the same sound, or an FM lead (**gap** until W-Core · Wave). Vary a few arp steps;
   with two leads, alternate call, pause and answer.
3. Arrangement: room for the intro, layers in stages, the main motif readable; if the drop loses impact, delay or
   lower a secondary layer.
Ask: "Plan a hi-tech drop where two beeps alternate. Keep kick and bass." Listen: the pulse holds and each answer has room.

**Psytrance — groove and continuity of the theme.**
1. Base: kick/bass relation, then percussion with accents; never change sample, gain and pattern at once.
2. Motif: a lead attack as anticipation in the intro or break; confirm the WAV's root note; compare short with a
   delay/reverb tail; after the lead enters, an answer in the gaps.
3. Substyle: full-on, twilight and progressive have their own profiles (styles).
Ask: "Plan a psytrance intro that announces this lead with a short hit." Listen: the timbre is recognisable and the tail leaves room for the motif.

**Dark — weight, texture and tension.**

title: Technique cards · Paths per style (2)
text:
| Direction | Production choice | Core plugins | What to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Darkpsy | A sustained dark texture behind, a lead or accent in front; formant, resonance or slow modulation on one track | GROWL, Core FX Modulate (*Tension phaser*), `filter`, F-Core *Atmosphere* | Movement separates the layers; kick/bass stay readable |
| Dark psycore | A glitch fill from a lead attack (repeats, accents, pauses); metallic body in the mids of one layer, protecting the sub | GLITCH, METAL, BODY | The fill ends before the next entry; bass notes fit the real BPM |
| Dark hi-tech | The workshop order: KBBB base, tension pause, ambience vs lead contrast, gradual entry, dialogue of timbres | W-Core, P-Core, SPACE, R-Core | One stage at a time; check the drop's entry and Undo |
| Slambient | Turn an attack into a long texture and let the tail fall back before the bass returns | SPACE, R-Core, F-Core *Atmosphere* | The texture keeps its identity without hiding the pulse |

**Common decisions.**

| When you ask for… | Core checks and decides |
|---|---|
| Another sample | Search the real library (sample database) and compare two candidates by role, attack, tail, note and BPM; pre-listen before swapping |
| Another effect | Name the missing job (body, movement, space) and pick the Core plugin for it from the catalogue; compare one at a time at matched gain |
| An impact, riser or texture | Reuse a sound of the track when it fits; F-Core *Impact* / *Build-up* / *Downlifter*; Bounce / Resample to keep a processed tail; reverse is a **gap** |
| A mix review | Find the track and region, compare with bypass at matched gain, check more than one section; start at the track that causes it |

title: Technique cards · Dark hi-tech: from the base to a dialogue of timbres (1)
text:
Teaching priority: high (Diogo). Source: a transcribed Ableton workshop by Vinícius; exact patch values not given.

1. **KBBB base (00:00:51–00:14:19).** 160 BPM in the demo (he usually works above 170–180). Kick and three bass hits
   per beat on a 1/16 grid, bass notes slightly shorter to control overlaps; a small variation in the first half;
   moderate saturation for mid/high body without boosting the lows. In Core: a W-Core bass preset or the Sampler + P-Core *KBBB*, BODY or
   `saturation`. A sixteenth lasts 93.75 ms at 160 BPM and 83.33 ms at 180. Compare kick, bass and sum before
   choosing a shorter kick, another bass articulation or ducking.
2. **Drums and a short pause (00:14:19–00:27:24).** Closed hat by the kick, open hat on the off-beat, a supporting
   snare/clap; velocity variation, a short 1/32 run, a lower second hit in a pair. Try dropping the bass for a moment
   to make room for another element. In Core: P-Core hats and build patterns; isolate the region if patterns are shared.
3. **Ambience vs FM lead (00:29:39–00:45:31).** A long note with modulation, reverb and peak control behind; a lead
   with oscillator modulation, filter movement and arp in front. In Core: F-Core *Atmosphere* + R-Core for the
   ambience; the FM lead is W-Core (*Glass FM Lead*, or FM in Colour) with a filter LFO.
4. **An entry that does not spend the drop (00:48:50–01:09:31).** A crash or impact marks an entry; a reversed crash
   anticipates it (reverse: **gap**; use a prepared WAV). Keep the intro bass repetitive, open the filter, save the
   note variation for the drop; bring elements in gradually; delay at the end of an ambience (D-Core).
5. **Make the timbres talk (01:30:37–01:40:48).** Loop a small region; cut or alternate passages of different
   timbres instead of letting one sound fill the section. Bounce / Resample helps edit the cuts. Check pan in mono.

title: Technique cards · Dark hi-tech: from the base to a dialogue of timbres (2)
text:
Ask: "Make these two leads talk for four bars. Keep kick and bass and leave a pause before the answer." First test
order: KBBB fit in a short region → a short drum pause → call and answer, then the transition.

title: Technique cards · Hi-tech: give room to the sounds that carry the section
text:
Source: intro of Paralocks' course (Alien Noise Academy). Restraint lets sounds stand out and hit harder. When a drop
feels full but undefined, find the element that should be in front and the layers that coincide with its entry.
Compare with a version where a secondary layer enters later, plays less or sits lower. Ask: "The hi-tech drop is full
but lost impact. Which secondary layer would you remove in the first phrase? One proposal only."

title: Technique cards · Hi-tech arrangement: room for the intro and bounce with effects
text:
Source: a Bitwig arrangement session. Duplicate the existing block as a starting point and reserve room for the intro;
choose when kick, bass and drums enter. Make an ambience from a small audio fragment with reverb; if the tail works,
**Bounce / Resample** a version that includes the effect and the full tail, keeping the editable source. Do not run it
through the same reverb again by accident.

title: Technique cards · Hi-tech: beep and pluck from one sound
text:
Source: a Bitwig Poly Grid session. A square wave and a simple arp; a triangle modulating the square's phase for a
more robotic timbre; the envelope turns a sustained beep into a short pluck. Test stereo modulation apart; compare a
fixed arp with one where a few steps change. In Core: **gap** for phase modulation until W-Core · Wave; today vary
the envelope and `filter` of the engine instrument, and vary a few MIDI steps with P-Core. Both articulations should
keep a recognisable timbre and the pulse.

title: Technique cards · Pick a kick and control the stereo low end
text:
Source: an Ableton Simpler excerpt. Pick a kick, place one hit per beat (4/4 = four per bar), start at a moderate level,
set it against the bass, check sum and peaks. In Core: the built-in `kick` instrument (pitch and decay per style) or a
library one-shot in the Core Sampler, with PUNCH for click and cut. The tutorial high-passes only the **Side** of an
M/S EQ on the master; Core's engine EQ has no Side mode (**gap**). Find the track that makes the stereo low end and
use `utility` *monoBelow* there before touching the master.

title: Technique cards · Percussion: groove, layers and resampling
text:
Source: an Ableton tutorial.
- A simple hat pattern first; when adding closed hats or shaker, check the group level; velocity for accents, gain
  for the track; vary the end of the second phrase.
- Two different claps with aligned attacks and opposite pan; compare with a single clap, check mono, keep the tail
  short if it hides the groove; Bounce / Resample with a final fade to reuse it.
- If a loop does not sit on the grid, tell a tempo mismatch from a pitch mismatch (the audio clip's *Fit to the song's
  BPM* and *Change pitch*).
- Width, parallel compression and reverb as separate experiments (SPACE, `compressor` with mix), each against bypass
  and in mono.

title: Technique cards · FX: textures, risers, voice and impacts
text:
Source: an Ableton tutorial.
- A texture that evolves slowly with formant and resonance movement: GROWL (vowel), Core FX Modulate, `filter` automation; a
  continuous and a gated version (PULSE).
- A crash into a riser: copy, long reverb, Bounce with the full tail, reverse (**gap**: use a prepared WAV), fade in,
  align the end with the transition. F-Core *Build-up* is the Core-native riser path.
- Voice by phrases: cut, set local gain, align key words to the grid; pitch or granular on chosen words (granular:
  **gap**, W-Core).
- A boom from an isolated kick or a spacious impact from a clap: long reverb on a copy (SPACE *huge*, R-Core), filter
  by role, control only the tail if it competes with the groove. F-Core *Impact*.
- Layer a short version and progressively slower versions of one sound into a texture.

title: Technique cards · Long synth one-shots: attack, tail and arrangement
text:
Source: an Ableton tutorial. Bounce a note or phrase with time for the tail; trim a copy, fade where it clicks, try
filter movement before adding effects; look for harsh resonances after saturation. Keep a normal and a reversed
version (reverse: **gap**). When reusing a tonal hit, confirm its source note before transposing (D♯ → G is +4
semitones **if** D♯ is the source). If the tail covers the kick, lower only the tail: `compressor` with sidechain from
the kick, or gain automation on the tail. Spread long hits as calls and answers with gaps.

title: Technique cards · Turn a lead pluck into an intro texture
text:
Source: a Cubase tutorial (Thorn sound), 2026-11-05. Announce a lead's timbre with an atmospheric hit at the start of
a bar, in the intro or before the lead returns.
1. Keep the source; Bounce one lead attack to audio, with a known note.
2. Load it in the Core Sampler with the sample's **own note** as root.
3. Keep a short version with a defined attack.
4. Make a long version with delay and reverb (D-Core, R-Core, or F-Core *Atmosphere*); compare with and without
   distortion; filter after distortion if needed.
5. Place it at the bar start, leaving room for the lead's entry; compare short and long at similar level.

title: Technique cards · Recipes for psycore, psytrance and slambient
text:
Research 2026-11-05; sources: producers' tutorials (Dash Glitch, E-Clip, Boomland), manufacturer docs, listening
references (Sonic Hypnosis Records).
- **Psycore glitch fill from a theme sound.** A short attack or syllable as a WAV; retriggers, accents and pauses make
  a short answer to the lead; vary one thing (retrigger speed, last accent). In Core: GLITCH, or repeated notes/rolls on
  a sampler track. Check the fill ends before the next important attack.
- **Psytrance motif, anticipation hit and answer.** Reuse one lead attack before the full motif; after it enters, a
  short answer in its gaps, same timbre family, different articulation.
- **Kick and bass with two comparable versions.** Change one thing: the bass note length or position against the
  kick's tail. Kick alone, bass alone, sum, at the same level, at the section's real notes and BPM. No fixed offset,
  universal phase or common gate.
- **Slambient: an attack into a layer across the section.** A dark or metallic attack (METAL); a long tail on its own
  track (SPACE *haunted*, R-Core); Bounce a controlled version; gradual entry and an exit before the next section.
  Infinite-reverb tricks from third-party reverbs are replaced by a tail with a controlled end.

title: Technique cards · Psytrance at 145 BPM: a whole track from an FL Studio tutorial (1)
text:
Source: a transcribed FL Studio psytrance tutorial given by Diogo on 2026-11-07 (timestamps `mm:ss` below; no patch
values). Status `externo`; each Core translation is `hipotese` until heard. Only what the manual did not have yet.

**Kick: punchy and laser.** A hybrid of a punchy dance kick and a long, clearly falling sine (`00:56`). In Core: the
engine `kick` with a longer pitch decay and amp decay (the sine tail), plus PUNCH *Kick click* for the attack; ZAP only if
the fall needs more laser. Check the tail ends before the next bass 16th.

**Fills come from a copy of the last repeat.** Repeat the pattern in powers of two, then make the last clip its own
pattern and change only that one (`02:14`–`02:30`). In Core: right-click the last clip > **Make independent copy**, then on its
last kick notes **Edit ▾ > STUTTER** (the tutorial's chop tool, `02:51`): a roll that "almost sounds like a note".

**The one-note 16th bass.** Most psytrance bass is one note in 16ths (`04:08`). The kick drowns the first 16th of each
beat: some producers delete it (KBBB), this tutorial keeps it and lets the velocities rise toward the end of every beat
(`04:21`–`04:36`). In Core: the Patterns window, shape KBBB or all four 16ths on the root; there is no velocity-ramp tool yet
(**gap**: set each note's velocity with the wheel). This is the same open choice as the 95/108/120 crescendo in
styles/psytrance.md: compare both by ear.

**Mark a phrase end with a moving comb.** A phaser in harmonic mode, standing still, mix up, its width automated, gives a
decaying comb filter at the end of a phrase (`04:50`–`05:24`). In Core: **+ Add effect** > **Filters** > **Comb at
the phrase ends · 8 bars** (or 16) does exactly this: a comb filter whose mix rises on the last bar of every phrase.
For a comb in the song's key, METAL (a damped comb tuned to Note = the bass root) with its Mix automated (its **A** button).

title: Technique cards · Psytrance at 145 BPM: a whole track from an FL Studio tutorial (2)
text:
**Bass that turns square.** Removing the even harmonics makes the bass hollow, like a square wave (`05:43`–`07:10`);
the tutorial builds it with an inverted delay at the root an octave up and automates how much is mixed in. In Core:
a W-Core bass (*Saw Roller*) with a square or PWM wavetable on Osc 2, and a link (**+ Ligação**) from a macro to the
mix of the two, automated for the change. A mix-in of only the odd harmonics on any sound is a **gap**.

**Short laser synths on the rhythm.** Three saws, a fast falling pitch envelope, a bit crusher for aliasing, then reverb
and delay (`07:20`–`07:45`); used now and then on accents. In Core: W-Core *Laser Zap* or *Laser Stab*, or a saw with
Unison 3 and an ENV 2 → pitch link (**+ Ligação**) with a short decay for the fall, **Filter+ Crush** or Core FX's Lo-fi
module for the aliasing, then **Reverb · SPACE** and **Delay · ECHO** (R-Core, D-Core).

**Phrygian dominant outside the drop.** Psytrance often sits in Phrygian dominant in the intro and breaks (`07:55`): a
chopped vocal with that sound, doubled by a flute. In Core: **Scale for P-Core** > Phrygian dominant for the lead; the clip
editor's **Slice** or VOICE STUTTER for the vocal; a flute is a **gap** (no flute in the library; the 2 *Orchestral
Psytrance* samples are the nearest).

**Arrangement in two 32-bar blocks.** 32 bars of intro, 32 of drop (`08:45`). Intro: a slow, subdued pad that follows the
flute's pattern (W-Core *Dawn Strings*, Mode Poly), a 303-style acid line (W-Core *Squelch 303* or *Acid Needle*:
Mono with Glide, Filter Bite up), shakers. Second half of the drop: add a drum break loop, a screaming 303 bass loop and more percussion
layers, to lift it without a new section. Stage's song shapes use 8 and 16-bar sections: make the two 32-bar blocks by hand
or as Intro 32 + Drop 32 on the ruler.

title: Technique cards · Psytrance at 145 BPM: a whole track from an FL Studio tutorial (3)
text:
**909 snare roll into the drop.** A snare on every 16th step, its velocity and pitch rising (`10:00`). In Core:
**Edit ▾ > Build-up > On a new track (snare from the library)** writes the roll with velocity rising 0.35 → 1; the
pitch rise is a **gap** (Transpose the last notes by hand, or put F-Core *Build-up* on that track). Then add a few
purpose-built FX and careful automation.

Ask: "Make a 145 BPM psytrance sketch: 32 bars intro in Phrygian dominant, 32 bars drop with one-note 16th bass, a
STUTTER kick fill on the last repeat and a snare build-up into the drop. Keep it near −17 LUFS."

title: Technique cards · Psytrance at 140 BPM: acid lead and a two-breakdown arrangement (1)
text:
Source: a second transcribed psytrance tutorial given by Diogo on 2026-11-07 (Serum, timestamps `mm:ss`; no values).
Status `externo`; each Core translation is `hipotese`. Only what the manual and the 145 BPM card above lack.

**A rolling bass in layers for the whole spectrum.** One rolling preset plus a few layers so the bass fills sub to top
(`00:28`–`01:06`). In Core: W-Core *Saw Roller* or *Saw Roller Low* with its **Sub** for the bottom; for the top,
**+ Wave** (a second Wave on the same track, Unison and Detune up, Sub off), or a second track with the same notes and
BODY or GROWL (they work above about 150 Hz, so the sub stays alone and mono).

**The acid lead, step by step** (`01:49`–`03:22`). In the W-Core window, Mode **Mono** (one note, legato):
1. **Octave** −2 (W-Core goes from −2 to +2).
2. **ENV 1** (the volume) with a quick Attack, a short Decay and a low Sustain.
3. A band-pass filter type, and **Bite** up for the resonance; an ENV 2 → Tone link (**+ Ligação**) for the opening
   on each note.
4. **Colour · Noise** a little.
5. Cut the lows: **+ Add effect** > **Filters** > High-pass, or a Core EQ low cut after the synth, so the bass keeps
   the bottom.
6. In **MATRIX**, **+ Ligação** from LFO 1 to the filter's Tone, Rate **1/4** synced (the tutorial's "rate four"), so
   the sound keeps changing.
7. In the notes: overlap a few notes so **Glide** slides between them (the tutorial's pitch bends), and put some notes
   an octave up (piano roll **Edit ▾ > Variation > Octave jumps (some notes)**). Then **Delay · ECHO** and **Reverb ·
   SPACE** so it stands out.

title: Technique cards · Psytrance at 140 BPM: acid lead and a two-breakdown arrangement (2)
text:
**Section moves.** A B section with a vocal sample (`04:08`); between sections, drum one-shots with a lot of delay
(a drum hit on its own track sent to D-Core *Throw 1/4*, or a Core FX Delay region with high feedback, on the last beat); after the
drop, take the top melody and the vocal out and bring in other synths, so the song moves on without a new tempo.

**Breakdown, build-up and a second breakdown.** The breakdown starts with a mysterious chord progression and a lot of
ambience (`05:21`): W-Core Mode **Poly** (up to 8 notes) on chords of the song's scale, **Reverb · SPACE** (R-Core),
**FX ▾** > Atmosphere. The build-up brings in the drop's elements one by one (`06:26`): in Stage's grid, switch them on a few
bars apart before the drop. A spoken-word sample over the build-up (`07:02`) goes on an audio track. The second
breakdown uses a different bass sound and tribal drums for tension (`07:20`–`07:40`): another W-Core bass preset on a
copy of the bass track; tribal drums are a **gap** (no tribal sample in the library yet; perc one-shots with the
Patterns window are the nearest).

Ask: "Write a 140 BPM psytrance acid lead on W-Core: Lead mode, octave −2, band filter with resonance, LFO 1 on the
filter at 1/4, a few slides and octave jumps. Keep it under the bass and near −17 LUFS."

title: Technique cards · Review the master and the synths before export
text:
Source: a tutorial excerpt (its "−10" is ambiguous; never use it as a target). Loop a section while trying EQ, light
compression and limiting, then check other sections before exporting; the analyser helps find differences, the ear
decides. A sub-sonic cut near 20 Hz only if there is a sub problem. If hats, crash or a synth cause the excess, start
at that track: parallel compression and width on the synths, checked in mono. Ask: "Review the master in this drop and
the break. Tell me if the excess comes from the synths or the master chain and propose one change at a time. Don't
apply yet."

title: Technique cards · What to log
text:
Template, BPM, region, Core version, function calls, values, the result, Undo, and the listening feedback per property
("like the rhythm", "don't like the timbre", "good elasticity", "too bright", "lost body", "good alone, bad with
kick"). A card is candidate knowledge; feedback is separate evidence. Only Diogo's own executed and checked examples
go to training.

title: 01 — Audio basics
text:
# 01 — Audio basics

The base the other chapters use to justify decisions. It comes from the workshop transcripts and is written as
teaching material; it is the most stable layer of the collection because it is physics, not taste.

title: 01 — Audio basics · Established
text:
- Inside Core, sound is a sequence of numbers — the amplitude over time. Two channels = stereo. A `sample` here is
  one measurement, not a file from a pack (`inbox/AICORE-flat/01-fundamentos-audio.md`).
- ADC/DAC, sample rate (48 kHz = 48 000 measurements per second) and bit depth (24 bits ≈ 16.7 million values) are
  technical project settings, not creative decisions
  (`01-fundamentos-audio.md`:27-37).
- A value goes from -1 to 1, `0` is silence, and when several tracks play their signals add up — that is where
  clipping comes from. Before recommending a sound, ask: how many sources play, where each one sits in the spectrum,
  whether the sum makes peaks, and whether the problem is level, frequency, phase or arrangement
  (`01-fundamentos-audio.md`:39-56).
- Frequency, fundamental and harmonics; the FFT as the bridge between time and spectrum
  (`inbox/AICORE-flat/02-frequencia-espectro-harmonicos.md`);
  sine/saw/square as starting points for timbre (`inbox/AICORE-flat/03-formas-onda-e-sintese.md`);
  phase and what an EQ does to the spectrum (`inbox/AICORE-flat/04-fase-e-eq.md`).
- Low end in the centre: on the master, a mid/side EQ with a high-pass **only on the sides**, so the low stereo
  information does not compete with kick and bass. The transcript gives no cutoff or slope — do not invent them
  (`inbox/AICORE-flat/07-master-e-low-end.md`:5-26). In Core, the
  master's Utility does this with *Mono below* (the templates use 20–110 Hz; see the template pages).

title: 01 — Audio basics · How to decide, with this base
text:
For every element, the questions the material asks
(`inbox/AICORE-flat/05-aplicacao-psytrance.md`:38-49):

1. What is the sound's musical role?
2. Which frequency range and which fundamental do we want?
3. Which waveform or source is a good starting point?
4. Which harmonics does it need to be heard?
5. Which elements does it compete with?
6. Which processing fits, and why?
7. How is it checked by ear, on the spectrum and in mono?

title: 01 — Audio basics · Source and limits
text:
Chapters 01–04 of the transcripts describe what was seen in a transcribed introductory class; 05 is an applied
inference for AICORE's goal; 07 is a procedure seen in another transcript. The source file separates what was seen
from what is inferred, and warns that the sub, bass, lead and conflict-analysis advice was not taught explicitly
(`inbox/AICORE-flat/06-fonte-e-limites.md`:11-29). The list of
"missing information" (`05-aplicacao-psytrance.md`:50-61) — the
kick/bass relation, patterns, envelopes, structure, loudness, audio examples — was open at the time.

text:
That list is now covered by chapters 02 to 10 and the style sheets. What is still missing is what is missing
everywhere: **annotated audio examples and human evaluation criteria**. The collection holds no before/after

title: 02 — Kick and bass
text:
# 02 — Kick and bass

The pair that defines the style. In Core the separation is **grammatical** (the bass ends before the next kick), not
ducking. This is `decisao_diogo`, and the most repeated rule in the whole collection.

title: 02 — Kick and bass · Established (1)
text:
**The KBBB family.** A kick at the start of each beat and three bass notes on the following sixteenths; KBB and K-B-B
with a rest are variants. Short envelopes: each note ends before the next and never overlaps the kick
(`estilos/geral.md:15`). KBBB is timing — it does not
define timbre; "elastic" is how the articulation is perceived, not a parameter
(`AICORE/docs/knowledge/KBBB-E-ELASTIC-BASS.md:7`).

**Grid and numbers.** PPQ 960, 1 beat = 960 ticks, 1/16 = 240, a 4/4 bar = 3840. Kick on steps [0, 4, 8, 12] of 16,
with a ghost on 15. Grooves in ticks inside each beat: `kbbb [240, 480, 720]`, `kbb [240, 480]`,
`kb-b [240, 720]`, `triplet [320, 640]`, `offbeat [480]`; velocities [0.9, 0.72, 0.8]
(`estilos/geral.md:17-18`) — all `codigo`.

**The gate.** `gateTicks = min(f × gap to the next event, gateMsTarget / msPerTick(section bpm))`, with
`gateMsTarget` of 25–50 ms (`estilos/geral.md:16`). Per
style, in the randomizer menus: dark psycore 32–45 ms, hi-tech 40–50, slambient 25–45, darkpsy 35–50, twilight
45–60, full-on 50–65, progressive 55–75
(`core-randomize.md`). Conversion: `1/16 = 15000/BPM` ms;
`gate = round(gateMs × BPM × PPQ / 60000)`. On W-Core the length of each bass note is the note's own gate plus `env1Decay`/`env1Release` (ms).

**Who owns the low end.** With no sub in the bass, the kick owns everything below ~80 Hz and the bass comes in with a
60–80 Hz high-pass (`estilos/hitech.md:68`,
`estilos/darkpsycore.md:72`). The accepted exception is
slambient, where the sub is the signature (0.7–0.85, octave −1)
(`estilos/slambient.md:45`). The open problem is phase:
above ~200 BPM the bass wave may not finish a cycle between notes, and the material calls it "the big challenge"
(`estilos/hitech.md:69`).

**Engine instrument values per style** (all `codigo`, measured in the templates):

title: 02 — Kick and bass · Established (2)
text:
| Style | Engine kick | Engine bass |
|---|---|---|
| Hi-tech | pitchStart 320–370, pitchEnd 52–58, pitchDecay 11–16, ampDecay 80–110, click 0.65–0.8, drive 0.28–0.38 (`hitech.md:44`) | envAmount 4.5–5.5, filterDecay 30–40, decay 40–48, release 5–7, drive 0.35–0.5, sub 0.2–0.3 (`hitech.md:45`) |
| Dark psycore | pitchStart 250–300, pitchEnd 44–50, pitchDecay 16–24, ampDecay 110–150, click 0.45–0.65, drive 0.3–0.45 (`darkpsycore.md:46`) | envAmount 4.5–5.8, filterDecay 30–45, decay 36–48, release 4–7, drive 0.4–0.65, sub 0.25–0.4 (`darkpsycore.md:47`) |
| Slambient | pitchStart 110–150, pitchEnd 34–40, ampDecay 65–115, click 0.02–0.08, drive 0.05–0.12 (`slambient.md:44`) | envAmount 2–3, filterDecay 35–45, release 6–9, sub 0.7–0.85, octave −1 (`slambient.md:45`) |

B-Core · Bass is gone (core-main #240, 2026-11-08): the bass is a sample of Diogo's in the **Sampler** or a **W-Core**
bass preset ([presets]../plugins/presets.md#w-core--wave)); each template page lists the exact kick and bass values
(templates).

**EQ and layers.** Kick layers: sub 40–70 Hz, body 100–250 Hz, click 2–8 kHz shorter than 30 ms; HP on the layers
without sub above 100 Hz; tune everything to the same tonic, octave or fifth; check the phase
(`geral.md:29`, `externo`). Kick EQ: a cut around 300 Hz and a
light lift around 1.5 kHz, with a narrow 2–3 dB dip at the bass fundamental (`geral.md:43`). Bass EQ: HP 35–45 Hz at
24 dB/oct, −3–5 dB at 55–80 Hz, +1–2 dB at 800 Hz–1.2 kHz, a dip around 300 Hz against mud (`geral.md:44`). The bass
decay is tuned to the tempo: at 142 BPM, ~80–110 ms (`geral.md:25`, `online`). For the click in Core: **PUNCH**.

**The elastic bass.** On W-Core the bounce comes from a short ENV 2 → `tone` (the pluck), a short amp envelope and
the gate; the bass presets (*Saw Roller*, *Full Speed Saw/Punch/Deep*, *Dark Plonk/Rubber/Bite*, *Deep Pulse*) are
the starting points ([presets]../plugins/presets.md#w-core--wave)). The 20 style racks are in
presets; all are `hypothesis`.

**The 12 bass constructions.** They live in two places with the same `id`: the intents in the AICORE guide
(`bass-variation-examples.json`) and the notes in Core's
pattern library (`patterns/bass/`, listed in P-Core). Names are as they appear
in the window:

title: 02 — Kick and bass · What the 2026 class asked for, and where the answer is now
text:
The transcript chapter on choosing a kick ends with a list of "criteria still missing"
(`inbox/AICORE-flat/08-escolha-do-kick-e-padrao-ritmico.md:29-39`):

| What it asked | Where the answer is | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Tail length | A drum one-shot must end (−40 dB from the peak) before the next beat; `sampleFit` and `regionFit` measure it (07) | `codigo` |
| Fundamental | Per style: hi-tech 45–48 Hz, dark psycore 54–59 Hz, slambient without click 34–40 Hz (above) | `codigo` |
| Kick pitch against the track's key | Kick layers tuned to the same tonic, octave or fifth (`geral.md:29`); know the sample's root before transposing (`ONE-SHOTS-LONGOS-DE-SYNTH.md`) | `externo` / to hear |
| Amount of sub and mids | `subRatio` (> 40 % below 120 Hz) and `centroidHz`, measured by Core's analyser; the words `sub`/`bright`/`dark` to filter (also in the sample database) | `codigo` |
| Timing against the bass | `regionFit`: every kick note against the next bass note, in ms, with `overlaps` and `shortestRoomMs` | `codigo` |
| Kicks across sub-genres | A full-on kick is longer and fuller than a dark psycore one; slambient has no click (styles) | `externo` |
| When to reject a kick | Several attacks do not work; a tail into the bass does not work; a wrong role is not fixed by hand (rejecting a kick does not change its category) | `codigo` |

**Still unanswered**: none of these criteria has been validated by a heard A/B. `regionFit` is arithmetic, not
listening, and the contract says so (`core-samples.md:161-164`).
